{{Short description|Matrix that, squared, equals itself}}
{{Use American English|date = January 2019}}
In [[linear algebra]], an '''idempotent matrix''' is a [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] which, when multiplied by itself, yields itself.<ref>{{cite book |last=Chiang |first=Alpha C. |title=Fundamental Methods of Mathematical Economics |publisher=McGraw–Hill |edition=3rd |year=1984 |page=[https://archive.org/details/fundamentalmetho0000chia_b4p1/page/80 80] |location=New York |isbn=0070108137 |url=https://archive.org/details/fundamentalmetho0000chia_b4p1/page/80 }}</ref><ref name=Greene>{{cite book |last=Greene |first=William H. |title=Econometric Analysis |publisher=Prentice–Hall |location=Upper Saddle River, NJ |edition=5th |year=2003 |pages=808–809 |isbn=0130661899 }}</ref> That is, the matrix <math>A</math> is idempotent if and only if <math>A^2 = A</math>. For this product <math>A^2</math> to be [[matrix multiplication|defined]], <math>A</math> must necessarily be a [[square matrix]]. Viewed this way, idempotent matrices are [[idempotent element (ring theory)|idempotent element]]s of [[matrix ring]]s.

==Example==
Examples of <math>2 \times 2</math> idempotent matrices are:
<math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}
3 & -6 \\
1 &  -2
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

Examples of <math>3 \times 3</math> idempotent matrices are:
<math display="block">
\begin{bmatrix}
 1 & 0 & 0 \\
 0 & 1 & 0 \\
 0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}
 2 & -2 & -4 \\
-1 &  3 &  4 \\
 1 & -2 & -3
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

==Real 2 × 2 case==
If a matrix <math>\begin{pmatrix}a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}</math> is idempotent, then
* <math>a = a^2 + bc,</math>
* <math>b = ab + bd,</math> implying <math>b(1 - a - d) = 0</math> so <math>b = 0</math> or <math>d = 1 - a,</math>
* <math>c = ca + cd,</math> implying <math>c(1 - a - d) = 0</math> so <math>c = 0</math> or <math>d = 1 - a,</math>
* <math>d = bc + d^2.</math>

Thus, a necessary condition for a <math>2\times2</math> matrix to be idempotent is that either it is [[diagonal matrix|diagonal]] or its [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]] equals 1.
For idempotent diagonal matrices, <math>a</math> and <math>d</math> must be either 1 or 0.

If <math>b=c</math>, the matrix <math>\begin{pmatrix}a & b \\ b & 1 - a \end{pmatrix}</math> will be idempotent provided <math>a^2 + b^2 = a ,</math> so ''a'' satisfies the [[quadratic equation]]
:<math>a^2 - a + b^2 = 0 ,</math> or <math>\left(a - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 + b^2 = \frac{1}{4}</math>

which is a [[circle]] with center (1/2, 0) and radius 1/2. In terms of an angle &theta;,
:<math>A = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 - \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & 1 + \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}</math> is idempotent.

However, <math>b=c</math> is not a necessary condition: any matrix
:<math>\begin{pmatrix}a & b \\ c & 1 - a\end{pmatrix}</math> with <math>a^2 + bc = a</math> is idempotent.

==Properties==
===Singularity and regularity===
The only non-[[singular matrix|singular]] idempotent matrix is the [[identity matrix]]; that is, if a non-identity matrix is idempotent, its number of independent rows (and columns) is less than its number of rows (and columns).

This can be seen from writing <math>A^2 = A</math>, assuming that {{mvar|A}} has full rank (is non-singular), and pre-multiplying by <math>A^{-1}</math> to obtain <math>A = IA = A^{-1}A^2 = A^{-1}A = I</math>.

When an idempotent matrix is subtracted from the identity matrix, the result is also idempotent. This holds since
:<math>(I-A)(I-A) = I-A-A+A^2 = I-A-A+A = I-A.</math>

If a matrix {{mvar|A}} is idempotent then for all positive integers n, <math>A^n = A</math>. This can be shown using proof by induction. Clearly we have the result for <math>n = 1</math>, as <math>A^1 = A</math>. Suppose that <math>A^{k-1} = A</math>. Then, <math>A^k = A^{k-1}A = AA = A</math>, since {{mvar|A}} is idempotent. Hence by the principle of induction, the result follows.

===Eigenvalues===
An idempotent matrix is always [[diagonalizable]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Horn|first=Roger A.|title=Matrix analysis|last2=Johnson|first2=Charles R.|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=1990|isbn=0521386322|page=[{{Google books|plainurl=y|id=PlYQN0ypTwEC|page=148|text=every idempotent matrix is diagonalizable}} p. 148]}}</ref> Its [[eigenvalue]]s are either 0 or 1: if <math>\mathbf{x}</math> is a non-zero eigenvector of some idempotent matrix <math>A</math> and <math>\lambda</math> its associated eigenvalue, then <math display="inline">\lambda \mathbf{x} = A \mathbf{x} = A^2\mathbf{x} = A \lambda \mathbf{x} = \lambda A \mathbf{x} = \lambda^2 \mathbf{x} ,</math> which implies <math>\lambda \in \{ 0, 1 \} .</math> This further implies that the [[determinant]] of an idempotent matrix is always 0 or 1. As stated above, if the determinant is equal to one, the matrix is [[Invertible_matrix#The_invertible_matrix_theorem|invertible]] and is therefore the [[identity matrix]].

===Trace===
The [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]] of an idempotent matrix—the sum of the elements on its main diagonal—equals the [[rank (linear algebra)|rank]] of the matrix and thus is always an integer. This provides an easy way of computing the rank, or alternatively an easy way of determining the trace of a matrix whose elements are not specifically known (which is helpful in [[statistics]], for example, in establishing the degree of [[bias (statistics)|bias]] in using a [[variance|sample variance]] as an estimate of a [[variance|population variance]]).

=== Relationships between idempotent matrices ===
In regression analysis, the matrix <math>M = I - X(X'X)^{-1} X'</math> is known to produce the residuals <math>e</math> from the regression of the vector of dependent variables <math>y</math> on the matrix of covariates <math>X</math>. (See the section on Applications.)  Now, let <math>X_1</math> be a matrix formed from a subset of the columns of <math>X</math>, and let <math>M_1 = I - X_1 (X_1'X_1)^{-1}X_1'</math>. It is easy to show that both <math>M</math> and <math>M_1</math> are idempotent, but a somewhat surprising fact is that <math>M M_1 = M</math>.  This is because <math>M X_1 = 0</math>, or in other words, the residuals from the regression of the columns of <math>X_1</math> on <math>X</math> are 0 since <math>X_1</math> can be perfectly interpolated as it is a subset of <math>X</math> (by direct substitution it is also straightforward to show that <math>M X = 0</math>). This leads to two other important results: one is that <math>(M_1 - M)</math> is symmetric and idempotent, and the other is that <math>(M_1 - M) M = 0</math>, i.e., <math>(M_1 - M)</math> is orthogonal to <math>M</math>. These results play a key role, for example, in the derivation of the F test.

Any [[Matrix_similarity|similar]] matrices of an idempotent matrix are also idempotent. Idempotency is conserved under a [[change of basis]]. This can be shown through multiplication of the transformed matrix <Math> S A S^{-1} </math> with <math>A</math> being idempotent: <math> (S A S^{-1})^2 =(S A S^{-1})(S A S^{-1}) = S A (S^{-1}S) A S^{-1}  = S A^2 S^{-1} = S A S^{-1}  </math>.

==Applications==
Idempotent matrices arise frequently in [[regression analysis]] and [[econometrics]]. For example, in [[ordinary least squares]], the regression problem is to choose a vector {{mvar|&beta;}} of coefficient estimates so as to minimize the sum of squared residuals (mispredictions) ''e''<sub>''i''</sub>: in matrix form,
: Minimize <math>(y - X\beta)^\textsf{T}(y - X\beta) </math>

where <math>y</math> is a vector of [[Dependent and independent variables|dependent variable]] observations, and <math>X</math> is a matrix each of whose columns is a column of observations on one of the [[Dependent and independent variables|independent variables]]. The resulting estimator is

:<math>\hat\beta = \left(X^\textsf{T}X\right)^{-1}X^\textsf{T}y </math>

where superscript ''T'' indicates a [[transpose]], and the vector of residuals is<ref name=Greene/>

:<math>
  \hat{e} = y - X \hat\beta
          = y - X\left(X^\textsf{T}X\right)^{-1}X^\textsf{T}y
          = \left[I - X\left(X^\textsf{T}X\right)^{-1}X^\textsf{T}\right]y
          = My.
</math>

Here both <math>M</math> and <math>X\left(X^\textsf{T}X\right)^{-1}X^\textsf{T}</math>(the latter being known as the [[hat matrix]]) are idempotent and symmetric matrices, a fact which allows simplification when the sum of squared residuals is computed:

:<math>\hat{e}^\textsf{T}\hat{e} = (My)^\textsf{T}(My) = y^\textsf{T}M^\textsf{T}My = y^\textsf{T}MMy = y^\textsf{T}My.</math>

The idempotency of <math>M</math> plays a role in other calculations as well, such as in determining the variance of the estimator <math>\hat{\beta}</math>.

An idempotent linear operator <math>P</math> is a projection operator on the [[column space|range space]] {{tmath|R(P)}} along its [[null space]] {{tmath|N(P)}}. <math>P</math> is an [[orthogonal projection]] operator if and only if it is idempotent and [[Symmetric matrix|symmetric]].
